props.title: Exodus

sections.content: Exodus (1960) stands as Otto Preminger's ambitious adaptation of Leon Uris's novel, chronicling the birth of Israel through an epic 3.5-hour narrative. Paul Newman delivers a commanding performance as Ari Ben Canaan, setting a template for Hollywood's portrayal of Israeli heroes that influenced later films like Cast a Giant Shadow (1966) and Munich (2005). The film's scope and Ernest Gold's Academy Award-winning score (including the iconic "Theme from Exodus") established a cinematic language for depicting Middle Eastern political struggles that resonates through to modern films like World War Z (2013) and Wonder Woman (2017).

sections.content: Preminger's direction broke new ground in how Hollywood approached Middle Eastern politics. Unlike the sensationalized orientalism of films like The Ten Commandments (1956), Exodus attempted a more nuanced portrayal of Arab-Jewish relations, though still through a decidedly Western lens. This influenced later films like The Little Drummer Girl (1984) and Paradise Now (2005), which increasingly explored the complexity of regional conflicts.

The film's production values set new standards for location shooting in Israel, predating the extensive Middle Eastern cinematography of Lawrence of Arabia (1962). Preminger's insistence on filming on location, despite numerous logistical challenges, created a visual authenticity that influenced decades of historical epics, from The Wind and the Lion (1975) to Kingdom of Heaven (2005). sections.content: Exodus marked a crucial shift in how Hollywood approached politically charged historical narratives. Its attempt to balance epic storytelling with complex political realities influenced films like The Battle of Algiers (1966) and Raid on Entebbe (1976). The film's treatment of terrorism, nationalism, and religious identity created a template for politically conscious blockbusters that continues through contemporary works like Body of Lies (2008) and Zero Dark Thirty (2012).
